result:
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the unpredictable timing of two or more processes touching the same resource, so the code works most of the time and fails only when they interleave badly. With a shared log, the symptom is lines from two writers spliced into each other, or lost entries.

Serialise the writers with `flock`:

```sh
{
  flock -x 9
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$msg" >&9
} 9>>/var/log/stockroom.log
```

The lock is released when the block ends and fd 9 closes, even if the script dies. Every writer must take the same lock, since `flock` is advisory and does nothing against a process that ignores it.

Always open with `>>`, never `>`: append mode makes the kernel seek to the end on each write, so writers cannot overwrite each other. A single short `printf` line in append mode is in practice written intact on a local filesystem even without the lock. You need the lock when one entry spans several writes or commands.

Avoid check-then-act patterns such as `[ -f "$log" ] || touch "$log"`, which are races themselves; `>>` already creates the file. On NFS, `flock` may be unreliable, so have a single process own the log there (for example, send entries through `logger` to syslog).
